{{Short description|Sequence of numbers with distinct sums}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Mian–Chowla sequence''' is an [[integer sequence]] defined
[[recursion|recursively]] in the following way. The sequence starts with

:<math>a_1 = 1.</math>

Then for <math> n>1</math>, <math>a_n</math> is the smallest integer such that every pairwise sum

:<math>a_i + a_j</math>

is distinct, for all <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> less than or equal to <math>n</math>.

==Properties==
Initially, with <math>a_1</math>, there is only one pairwise sum, 1 + 1 = 2. The next term in the sequence, <math>a_2</math>, is 2 since the pairwise sums then are 2, 3 and 4, i.e., they are distinct.  Then, <math>a_3</math> can't be 3 because there would be the non-distinct pairwise sums 1 + 3 = 2 + 2 = 4. We find then that <math>a_3 = 4</math>, with the pairwise sums being 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8. The sequence thus begins 
:[[1 (number)|1]], [[2 (number)|2]], [[4 (number)|4]], [[8 (number)|8]], [[13 (number)|13]], [[21 (number)|21]], [[31 (number)|31]], [[45 (number)|45]], [[66 (number)|66]], [[81 (number)|81]], [[97 (number)|97]], [[123 (number)|123]], [[148 (number)|148]], [[182 (number)|182]], [[204 (number)|204]], [[252 (number)|252]], [[290 (number)|290]], 361, 401, 475, ... {{OEIS|id=A005282}}.

==Similar sequences==
If we define <math>a_1 = 0</math>, the resulting sequence is the same except each term is one less (that is, 0, 1, 3, 7, 12, 20, 30, 44, 65, 80, 96, ... {{OEIS2C|id=A025582}}).

==History==
The sequence was invented by Abdul Majid Mian and [[Sarvadaman Chowla]].

==References==
* S. R. Finch, ''Mathematical Constants'', Cambridge (2003): Section 2.20.2
* R. K. Guy ''Unsolved Problems in Number Theory'', New York: Springer (2003)
